newsitem.title: USA: CPI target useful for Fed -- economist Cecchetti.
newsitem.headline: CPI target useful for Fed -- economist Cecchetti.

text.p: Targeting a Consumer Price Index (CPI) range would help the Federal Reserve make monetary policy more transparent and credible, Ohio State University Professor of Economics Stephen Cecchetti said on Monday.
Cecchetti, who wrote extensively about the usefulness of pegging monetary policy to a target, will become New York Fed Director of Research and Executive Vice President in August.
"It is important for monetary policy to be transparent. This is true both because policy has to be credible and for accountability," Cecchetti told Reuters.

"You want policy to be credible and policy makers to be accountable. Transparency serves both of those purposes," said Cecchetti, who as research director will advise New York Fed President William McDonough on monetary policy.

McDonough was the first Fed official to come up with a specific target for U.S. monetary policy when he spelled out last year that price stability would correspond to a core Consumer Price Index range between 0.5 and 2.0 percent.
"It's important for any central bank to make sure people in the country understand what central bankers are doing and why they are doing it," Cecchetti added.
"Having a target is the beginning of transparency. It helps explain what you are doing and why you are doing it," Cecchetti, a long-time supporter of Fed openness, also said.

"Having a target helps explain that something has happened in the economy, and that what you are doing is because you have a goal," pointed out Cecchetti, who will replace at the New York Fed director of research Frederic Mishkin.
Mishkin, who will resume teaching economics at Columbia University next fall, worked with McDonough on the notion of targeting a core CPI range to achieve a more credible and accountable policy.
Cecchetti acknowledged that one difficulty in pegging policy to a target was the choice of the appropriate target.

"It's a mistake to have a policy stating inflation should be between zero and 2.0 percent all of the time because this means that if inflation would go to 2.1 or 2.2 percent, you would be forced to tighten severely simply because you stated you have to stay under 2.0 percent," he added.

The Humphrey-Hawkins Act requires the Fed to seek balanced growth and maximum employment as well as price stability -- a dual mandate that, at times, raises questions about the U.S. central bank's objectives or policy actions.
Cecchetti said the time frame chosen to attain an inflation objective should be a key factor for policy and allow the Fed to still address near-term risks to the economy.

"The smartest thing to do is to state a target range, and with an horizon that is medium-term, which allows for some flexibility in dealing with the possible real side problems you're going to create," the Ohio State professor said.

"You don't want to sacrifice the real side of the economy on the short-run in order to hit your long-run inflation target," Cecchetti said, adding that specific inflation targets are impossible to hit and thus not credible.

"Targeting an inflation range is not about stating a hard and fast range because that's very dangerous for the real side of the economy and the repercussions are serious," stressed Cecchetti, pointing out the U.S. anti-inflation fight lacked the drive to force the CPI much below 3.0 percent.
"There are many people who feel that if you stabilize prices as much as you possibly can, then, the real sector is destabilized significantly," he added.
"There are policy arguments for weighting the real side as well," the future New York Fed director said, referring to the growth mandate contained in the Fed's Congressional act.
Althought the CPI has come under criticism for overstating inflation, Cecchetti said it was the best-known, most commonly used index that should serve to make policy more transparent.
